question: Explain DOM parsing, render tree construction, and script execution. What is the difference between <script>, <script async>, and <script defer>?
rubric: Explains HTML parsing into DOM tree and CSS parsing into CSSOM tree
Describes how DOM + CSSOM combine to form the Render Tree and Layout phase

Differentiates standard <script> (blocks parsing), async (fetches in parallel, executes immediately upon download blocking DOM), and defer (fetches in parallel, executes in order after DOM parsing completes)
Mentions DOMContentLoaded event timing relative to script loading
sampleAnswer:
When a browser requests an HTML document, it streams bytes and converts them to tokens, nodes, and the DOM tree in parallel with fetching external resources. In parallel, linked CSS files are parsed into the CSSOM. The browser combines DOM and CSSOM to create the Render Tree, which calculates layout dimensions and paints pixels.

Script Execution Modes:
1. Standard `<script>`: Pauses HTML parsing immediately, downloads the JS file synchronously, executes it, and then resumes HTML parsing. This blocks first contentful paint (FCP).
2. `<script async>`: Downloads the script asynchronously in parallel with HTML parsing. As soon as download finishes, HTML parsing pauses to execute the script immediately. Order of execution is non-deterministic.
3. `<script defer>`: Downloads the script asynchronously in parallel with HTML parsing, but delays execution until HTML parsing is fully complete (just before DOMContentLoaded). Preserves execution order.
codeSnippet:
<!-- Standard: Blocks parsing during download and execution -->
<script src="app.js"></script>

<!-- Async: Downloads parallel, pauses parsing to execute as soon as ready -->
<script async src="analytics.js"></script>

<!-- Defer: Downloads parallel, executes in DOM order after parsing finishes -->
<script defer src="main-bundle.js"></script>
commonPitfalls: Confusing async with defer regarding execution order
Assuming defer delays download rather than execution
Forgetting that async scripts execute out of order as soon as they finish downloading

question: How do <picture>, <source>, and srcset with sizes enable responsive media delivery and prevent layout shift?
rubric: Explains the difference between resolution switching (srcset) and art direction (<picture>)
Describes how the 'sizes' attribute gives layout hints to the browser before CSS layout executes
Explains aspect-ratio or explicit width/height attributes for preventing Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
sampleAnswer: Responsive images use two main patterns: 1. Resolution Switching (`srcset` + `sizes` on ``): Allows browser to choose the ideal image resolution based on device pixel ratio (DPR) and layout viewport width. The `sizes` attribute tells the preloader how wide the image will render before CSS loads. 2. Art Direction (`` element): Used when image crop or format (AVIF, WebP, JPEG) must change depending on viewport media queries or browser format support. To prevent CLS, always provide explicit `width` and `height` attributes on the `` tag so the browser computes the aspect-ratio slot before the image downloads.

Using <picture> for simple resolution changes when srcset + sizes is cleaner

question: Explain Block Formatting Context (BFC), Stacking Contexts (z-index), and Container Queries vs Media Queries.
rubric: Defines BFC and lists triggers (display: flow-root, overflow: hidden, flex/grid items, position: fixed/absolute)
Explains how BFC prevents margin collapsing and clears floats
Explains Stacking Context creation (position + z-index, opacity < 1, transform, filter, isolation: isolate)
Compares Container Queries (@container) targeting parent element width vs Media Queries (@media) targeting viewport width
sampleAnswer:
A Block Formatting Context (BFC) is an isolated visual layout region where child blocks are laid out vertically. Forming a BFC (e.g. via `display: flow-root`) contains internal floats without clearfix hacks and prevents vertical margins from collapsing with elements outside the BFC.

A Stacking Context determines rendering order along the Z-axis. Child elements with `z-index: 9999` will still render behind an element with `z-index: 1` if their parent belongs to a lower stacking context. Stacking contexts are formed by `isolation: isolate`, `opacity < 1`, `transform`, `filter`, or `position` with non-auto `z-index`.

Container Queries (`@container`) evaluate the size of a designated parent container rather than the browser viewport (`@media`), making modular component design truly context-aware when placed in sidebars, modals, or grid columns.
commonPitfalls: Assuming high z-index overrides parent stacking contexts
Using overflow: hidden solely to clear floats instead of display: flow-root

question: How do CSS Grid and Flexbox differ in terms of 1D vs 2D layout calculation algorithms?
rubric: Identifies Flexbox as 1D (content-driven layout along main/cross axis) vs Grid as 2D (layout-driven rows and columns)
Explains flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis sizing math
Explains grid-template-columns with minmax(), fr units, and auto-fit/auto-fill
sampleAnswer:
Flexbox is designed for 1-dimensional layouts (a single row or column at a time) where children drive the layout size based on content. CSS Grid is designed for 2-dimensional layouts where the parent container defines a structured grid coordinate system of rows and columns.

In Flexbox, space distribution is calculated via `flex-basis`, `flex-grow`, and `flex-shrink`. In CSS Grid, track sizing uses fractional units (`fr`) alongside dynamic functions like `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr))` to create responsive layouts without media queries.
commonPitfalls: Using Flexbox with hardcoded width percentages when CSS Grid is better suited
Confusing auto-fit (stretches tracks to fill remaining space) with auto-fill (creates empty tracks)

question: Explain the JavaScript Event Loop, Call Stack, Microtask queue, and Macrotask queue with execution order examples.
rubric: Describes single-threaded call stack execution
Identifies Microtasks (Promise.then, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver)
Identifies Macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI rendering)
Explains that ALL microtasks in the queue drain completely before the next macrotask or browser paint
sampleAnswer:
JavaScript runs on a single-threaded event loop. Code execution starts on the synchronous Call Stack. When asynchronous tasks complete, their callbacks enter queue structures:

1. Microtask Queue: Holds Promise reactions (`.then`), `queueMicrotask`, and `MutationObserver`. The Event Loop drains the ENTIRE microtask queue before moving to the next task or triggering a screen repaint.
2. Macrotask Queue: Holds `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, network I/O, and UI events. The Event Loop processes ONE macrotask, then drains all microtasks that were queued, then yields to rendering if necessary, then picks the next macrotask.
commonPitfalls: Believing setTimeout(fn, 0) executes immediately before Promises
Not realizing an infinite loop of microtasks will starve the event loop and freeze UI rendering
followUpQuestions: Where does requestAnimationFrame fit relative to microtasks and browser painting?

question: How do Closures and Garbage Collection work in V8? Give an example of a memory leak caused by uncleaned closures.
rubric: Defines Closure as a function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment
Explains V8 Mark-and-Sweep garbage collection and root reachability
Demonstrates closure memory leak (shared scope retainment)
sampleAnswer:
A closure is formed when an inner function retains references to variables in its outer lexical scope, even after the outer function has returned. V8 uses a Mark-and-Sweep garbage collector: objects are eligible for GC when they are no longer reachable from root objects.

In V8, functions in the same lexical parent scope share a single closure scope object. If one inner function holds a reference to a huge object, and another inner function is kept alive, the huge object CANNOT be garbage collected.
commonPitfalls: Assuming garbage collection cleans up unused local variables even if a sibling closure in the same scope remains referenced
Forgetting to detach event listeners or clear setInterval callbacks in SPA navigation
followUpQuestions: How do WeakMap and WeakSet prevent memory leaks compared to Map and Set?

question: How does React Fiber reconciliation work? How do concurrent features like useTransition and useDeferredValue prioritize render lanes?
rubric: Explains Fiber architecture as a linked list tree representation supporting interruptible, incremental rendering
Differentiates Render Phase (pure, asynchronous, interruptible) vs Commit Phase (synchronous DOM mutation)
Explains Lane Priority System (Sync lane vs InputContinuous vs Transition lane)
Describes how useTransition yields control to high-priority user inputs
sampleAnswer:
React Fiber replaced the synchronous stack reconciler with a linked-list data structure where every component instance is a 'Fiber node'. Fiber allows React to split rendering work into small chunks, pause work to handle urgent user input, and resume or discard work as priorities change.

Two Main Phases:
1. Render Phase: React traverses Fiber nodes, calls component functions, and calculates diffs. This phase is pure, async, and can be interrupted or restarted.
2. Commit Phase: React synchronously applies calculated mutations to the DOM and fires layout effects.
commonPitfalls: Performing side effects inside the Render phase
Confusing useTransition (for state update triggers) with useDeferredValue (for wrapping received prop values)

question: Compare React Server Components (RSC) vs Client Components. What are the rules for serializability across boundaries?
rubric: Explains RSC execute purely on the server, zero client bundle size impact, direct DB access
Explains Client Components ('use client') run on server for SSR and hydrate on client for interactivity
Explains serializability rule: Props passed from Server Components to Client Components must be serializable
sampleAnswer:
React Server Components (RSC) execute exclusively on the server during build or request time. They never ship their JavaScript code to the browser, allowing direct access to databases with zero bundle overhead.

Client Components (marked with `'use client'`) render on the server to generate HTML (SSR) and hydrate on the client to enable state (`useState`), side effects (`useEffect`), and event handlers (`onClick`).
commonPitfalls: Adding 'use client' at the top of every file out of habit
Attempting to pass non-serializable functions as props from RSC to Client Components

question: Explain Discriminated Unions, Type Narrowing, conditional types, and how the 'infer' keyword extracts types in generic utility functions.
rubric: Defines Discriminated Union with a common literal property tag
Explains Type Narrowing via switch/if guards and exhaustiveness checking using 'never'
Explains Conditional Types (T extends U ? X : Y)
Explains 'infer' keyword for pattern matching and extracting internal types within conditional types
sampleAnswer:
A Discriminated Union is a union of object types that share a single common literal property (the 'discriminant'). TypeScript narrows the specific object shape inside control flow blocks based on checks against that discriminant.

Conditional Types take the form `T extends U ? X : Y`. When combined with the `infer` keyword, TypeScript can extract sub-types dynamically during type inference.
commonPitfalls: Using non-literal properties as union discriminants
Forgetting exhaustiveness checking with 'never' when handling API response unions

question: What is the difference between type assertions (as), type guards (is), and unknown vs any?
rubric: Explains 'any' disables type checking vs 'unknown' enforces type checking before usage
Explains Type Assertions ('as') force compiler override without runtime checks
Explains Custom Type Guard functions using 'param is Type' predicate syntax for safe runtime validation
sampleAnswer:
`any` opts out of type safety completely. `unknown` represents an unknown type safely: TypeScript forces developers to perform runtime validation or type narrowing before accessing properties.

Type Assertion (`val as MyType`) tells the compiler to trust the developer's type assignment, but performs ZERO runtime validation.

Type Guard (`function isUser(val: unknown): val is User`) performs actual runtime property validation and returns a boolean.
commonPitfalls: Using 'as MyType' for untrusted network payloads instead of validating schemas
Using 'any' as a quick fix for complex generic type errors

question: How do you build a fully accessible modal dialog (WCAG 2.2 AA compliant)? Detail keyboard focus traps and screen reader roles.
rubric: Identifies key ARIA attributes: role='dialog', aria-modal='true', aria-labelledby, aria-describedby
Explains Focus Management: move focus into dialog on open, trap focus within dialog, restore focus on close
Mentions key bindings: Escape key to dismiss dialog
Explains hiding background content via inert attribute on app root
sampleAnswer:
An accessible modal dialog requires precise ARIA semantics, focus management, and keyboard event handling to pass WCAG 2.2 AA standards.

1. Markup & Semantics: `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`.
2. Focus Management: Save activeElement reference on open. Intercept `Tab` and `Shift+Tab` to trap focus within modal. Listen for `Escape` to close and restore focus.
3. Background Invalidation: Set `inert` or `aria-hidden="true"` on the main application container while modal is active.
commonPitfalls: Forgetting to restore focus to trigger button when modal closes
Allowing screen reader users to navigate background DOM behind modal

question: What are aria-live regions (polite vs assertive), and how do you announce dynamic SPA updates?
rubric: Defines aria-live attribute for screen reader notifications of dynamic DOM changes
Differentiates polite (waits for speech pause) vs assertive (interrupts current speech)
Explains aria-atomic='true' to announce entire region vs partial updates
sampleAnswer:
Single Page Applications (SPAs) update DOM content dynamically without full page reloads. Screen reader users need explicit announcements when state changes.

1. `aria-live="polite"`: Screen readers announce the update at the next natural speech pause.
2. `aria-live="assertive"`: Screen readers interrupt current speech immediately for urgent updates.
commonPitfalls: Overusing aria-live='assertive', annoying screen reader users with constant speech interruptions
Injecting dynamic content into an aria-live region before the region itself is rendered in DOM

question: Walk through diagnosing and optimizing Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) on a heavy e-commerce PDP.
rubric: Defines Core Web Vitals: LCP (< 2.5s), INP (< 200ms), CLS (< 0.1)
Diagnoses LCP bottlenecks: hero image optimization (fetchpriority='high', inline CSS, preloading)
Diagnoses INP bottlenecks: long tasks (>50ms) on main thread, yielding via scheduler.yield() or requestAnimationFrame
Diagnoses CLS bottlenecks: un-sized images, font swapping with size-adjust
sampleAnswer:
Core Web Vitals measure user-centric performance metrics:

1. LCP (Largest Contentful Paint - Goal < 2.5s): Set `fetchpriority="high"` on hero image, preload critical image URLs in HTML `<head>`, and serve AVIF/WebP over CDN.
2. INP (Interaction to Next Paint - Goal < 200ms): Break up long tasks (>50ms) into micro-tasks using `await scheduler.yield()`, move heavy non-UI processing to Web Workers.
3. CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift - Goal < 0.1): Reserve CSS aspect-ratio bounding boxes or skeleton layout slots for async content.
commonPitfalls: Lazy loading the LCP hero image (loading='lazy' causes severe LCP regression)
Focusing exclusively on Lighthouse lab data instead of real user monitoring field data

question: Explain how bundler tree-shaking works (ES Modules vs CommonJS) and how to diagnose bundle bloat.
rubric: Explains Tree-Shaking as dead code elimination based on static import/export analysis
Explains why ES Modules enable static analysis vs CommonJS dynamic execution
Explains sideEffects flag in package.json
Tools: rollup-plugin-visualizer, webpack-bundle-analyzer
sampleAnswer:
Tree-shaking is a bundler optimization technique that removes unused exports from the production JavaScript bundle. It relies on ES Module (ESM) static syntax (`import` and `export`), where module dependencies can be analyzed at compile-time before code execution.

CommonJS (`require()`) calls are dynamic and can be evaluated inside conditional loops at runtime, making static dependency graph analysis and dead-code elimination impossible or unsafe.
commonPitfalls: Importing CJS versions of packages (e.g. lodash instead of lodash-es)
Top-level side effects inside unused modules preventing bundlers from safely pruning them

question: Explain how to debug a subtle async race condition where network responses return out of order, and how AbortController solves it.
rubric: Explains Async Race Condition scenario (stale response overwriting latest UI state)
Explains AbortController and AbortSignal for fetch cancellation
Explains integration with React useEffect cleanup
sampleAnswer:
An async race condition occurs when multiple asynchronous network requests are triggered sequentially, but complete out of order due to network latency variations.

Solution using `AbortController`: Before issuing a new fetch request, abort the previous pending request signal. This instantly cancels the in-flight HTTP request at the browser layer and prevents out-of-order state updates.
commonPitfalls: Treating AbortError as an unhandled application error in catch blocks
Relying solely on local boolean flags without canceling HTTP network requests on the wire

question: Compare git rebase vs git merge. When should you use interactive rebase (git rebase -i), and how do you resolve conflicts?
rubric: Compares git merge (non-destructive 3-way merge commit) vs git rebase (re-applies commits on top of tip)
Explains Interactive Rebase (`git rebase -i HEAD~N`): squash, reword, fixup, drop
Steps to resolve conflicts during rebase (`git add .` -> `git rebase --continue`)
sampleAnswer:
`git merge` combines two feature branches by creating a new 'merge commit'. It is non-destructive and preserves complete historical context.

`git rebase` rewrites history by taking commits from your feature branch and re-applying them sequentially onto the tip of the target base branch.

Interactive Rebase (`git rebase -i HEAD~N`) allows engineers to clean up local feature branches (squash typos, reword messages) before submitting a PR.
codeSnippet:
# Interactive rebase for last 4 commits
git rebase -i HEAD~4

# Resolve conflict workflow:
git add src/components/Dashboard.tsx
git rebase --continue
commonPitfalls: Rebasing public shared branches that teammates are actively pulling from
Using 'git push -f' without '--force-with-lease'
followUpQuestions: What is the Golden Rule of Git Rebasing?

question: How does git bisect use binary search to locate regression bugs across a large codebase commit history?
rubric: Explains binary search algorithm applied to commit graph
Outlines manual bisect workflow: git bisect start -> git bisect bad -> git bisect good <commit>
Explains automated bisect using test scripts: git bisect run npm test
sampleAnswer:
`git bisect` is a built-in debugging tool that uses binary search to find the exact commit that introduced a bug or performance regression in a codebase.

Workflow:
1. Initialize: `git bisect start`
2. Mark current broken commit as bad: `git bisect bad`
3. Mark historical working commit as good: `git bisect good v1.2.0`
4. Git automatically checks out a commit halfway. You test, mark good/bad, and Git isolates the culprit commit.
codeSnippet:
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v2.4.0
git bisect run npm test -- --spec src/tests/cart.test.ts
commonPitfalls: Not resetting bisect state when finished (forgetting 'git bisect reset')
Testing commits where the project build fails due to unrelated broken dependencies
followUpQuestions: How do you skip unbuildable commits during a bisect session?

question: Design a scalable State Management & Caching strategy for a real-time collaborative workspace app (like Figma or Notion).
rubric: Architectural layers: UI View layer, Local Client Cache, Real-time Sync Engine, Persistence (IndexedDB)
Conflict Resolution: CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types like Yjs or Automerge)
Optimistic UI Updates: Immediate local state mutation with rollback queues
State Normalization: Normalized entity stores with ID lookup dictionaries
sampleAnswer:
Architecture Overview for Collaborative Workspace:
1. State Layer Separation: Local UI state (Zustand/Atomic), Shared Document Model (CRDTs), Server Cache (TanStack Query).
2. Real-time Synchronization: CRDT data structures for multi-user editing transmitted over WebSockets.
3. Offline-First: Sync local state to IndexedDB via Dexie.js for instant startup load times.
4. Performance: Normalize data tables (`{ ids: ['1'], entities: { '1': {...} } }`) to prevent cascading re-renders.
commonPitfalls: Storing deeply nested object trees directly in React state
Relying on last-write-wins (LWW) server timestamps for concurrent text editing

question: Compare Micro-frontends (Module Federation) vs Monorepo vs Monolith architectures for a multi-team engineering org.
rubric: Monolith: Single codebase, simple, but slow build times across large teams
Monorepo (Turborepo, Nx): Unified repository housing distinct applications and shared packages, atomic commits, shared CI caching
Micro-Frontends (Module Federation): Decoupled independently deployed applications combined at runtime, team autonomy
sampleAnswer:
Architectural Comparison:
1. Monolith: Simple DX, easy end-to-end refactoring, but long CI/CD build times as team grows.
2. Monorepo (Turborepo/Nx): Single source of truth with shared design packages (`@company/ui`). Atomic commits across app boundaries and shared CI caching.
3. Micro-Frontends (Webpack Module Federation): Independent team autonomy without coordinating deployment schedules, but higher operational overhead.
commonPitfalls: Adopting micro-frontends prematurely for small engineering teams
Allowing micro-frontend teams to run mismatched React major versions
